items.key: ai:i studied business, then became a pilot: why my degree did not define my career
items.text: I studied business, then became a pilot: Why my degree did not define my career
items.article: Dhriti Reddy studied entrepreneurship at Woxsen University before becoming a commercial pilot with IndiGo. She shares how family, school, university, international exposure and business education shaped her journey to the cockpit, and why she believes a degree should expand career possibilities rather than define a person’s professional future. - Article by Dhriti Reddy, Pilot, IndiGo Airlines, and BBA (Entrepreneurship Development) graduate from Woxsen University It was in my early teens that I first realised I was not simply a passenger travelling on an aircraft. I was fascinated by airplanes, the cockpit and the pilots. While most passengers looked forward to reaching their destination, I found myself fascinated by the aircraft itself and the professionalism of the cockpit crew. By the age of 13, I had made a firm decision: one day, I would become a pilot. What I did not know then was that the journey to the cockpit would not be a straight line. My undergraduate degree was in Business Management, specialising in Entrepreneurship Development, a field that, at first glance, seems far removed from aviation. Today, I realise it was never a detour. It was part of the preparation. HOW I MADE THE LEAP FROM BUSINESS TO AVIATION

items.key: ai:specific amount of deli meat associated with higher dementia risk in new review
items.text: Specific amount of deli meat associated with higher dementia risk in new review
items.article: Eating about two slices of deli meat daily was associated with substantially higher dementia and Alzheimer's risk, according to a new review of ultra-processed foods. New York-based registered dietitian Kelly Springer shares research on highly processed foods and explains how combining fruits, vegetables, nuts and other nutrient-rich options can support long-term health. Eating just two slices of deli meat a day was associated with a substantially higher risk of dementia, according to a new review of ultra-processed foods (UPFs) and brain health. The findings, published in the August 2026 issue of Annual Review of Nutrition, looked at dozens of human and animal studies, including one involving nearly 500,000 people in the U.K. The study found that each additional 25 grams of processed meat eaten daily corresponded with a 44% higher risk of all-cause dementia and a 52% higher risk of Alzheimer's. Twenty-five grams of processed meat equals roughly one to two slices of deli meat, depending on how thick the meat is sliced. JUST ONE SMALL SERVING OF ULTRA-PROCESSED FOOD A DAY LINKED TO HIGHER DISEASE RISK, MAJOR STUDY FINDS The review, done by an international team of 27 researchers, looked more broadly at whether diets high in UPFs may contribute to brain aging over time.

Over this period, the price has climbed from $802 million to $866 million. The contractor is suing its own designer and insurer for $400 million. items.key: ai:5 sarees from west bengal to add to your durga puja wardrobe
items.text: 5 sarees from West Bengal to add to your Durga Puja wardrobe
items.article: Besides being a festival of faiths, feasts and festivities, Durga Puja is also an exhibition of Bengali culture and craft. Dressing up in Bengali sarees cannot be replaced by anything else for this very reason! Be it the comfort of Tant or the luxury of Baluchari, Bengali traditional wear encapsulates Bengali ethos perfectly. So if you are going to celebrate Saptami, Ashtami, Navami or Dashami this year, take a close look at 5 traditional Bengali sarees from Bengal that you would not want to miss! If there's one saree that instantly transports you to a Bengali celebration, it's the Tant saree. Traditionally handmade from cotton, this saree is perfect for those blistering hot Puja days. The ever-so-classic white and red border tant saree is a must-have in any Bengali woman's festive wardrobe, especially during Durga puja. But, nowadays, tant sarees come in all shades of the rainbow! items.article: Pam Dawber was best known for her role as Mindy in the sitcom Mork & Mindy alongside Robin Williams in the late 1970s and early '80s, but what is she doing now? Explore her life, career and famous husband Pam Dawber won over viewers for her breakout role as Mindy McConnell in quirky seventies sitcom Mork & Mindy , alongside the late Robin Williams. But what is she doing now, almost 45 years after the show came to an end? From her marriage to another successful television star to family life and a break from the public eye, get to know more about what Pam is doing now after stepping away from Hollywood… After Mork & Mindy came to an end in 1982, Pam's next big role was starring as Samantha Russell on My Sister Sam between 1986 and 1988. Alongside her castmates, she filmed a public service announcement that led to the first anti-stalking law in the United States. items.text: Tunisia softens its ‘false news’ penalty. What really changed, and why now?
items.article: Fines replace jail terms for first-time ‘false news’ offences under a decree rights groups say is still repressive. Tunisia has softened a cybercrime law that has landed journalists and activists in prison, letting first-time offenders pay fines instead of serving time. The amendment to Decree 54, which went into effect on Wednesday, sets fines of 10,000 to 20,000 Tunisian dinars ($3,370 to $6,740) for a first offence of spreading “false news” and related violations. The fines replace a five-year prison sentence. However, repeat offenders may still face jail. Rights and media freedom advocates in Tunisia and abroad have long opposed the decree as repressive, saying it has been wielded against President Kais Saied’s opposition, activists and reporters. The government, meanwhile, says the decree protects people and public order from attack, and is needed to tackle online crime and disinformation. So what has changed, how has the decree been used, and why has Tunisia softened it now?
